headlines.article_text: Trump denies Musk claim he ordered Starlink restrictions in Ukraine Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week. Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on October 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. headlines.article_text: Netflix hires Peter Rice to run content. Here's what it means Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Netflix has replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with former Disney executive Peter Rice. Rice brings a wealth of experience in television and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports telecasts, prestige television and theatrical distribution. Netflix's viewership has stagnated in recent quarters. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday. In this article NFLX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:06 01:06 Netflix’s big executive shakeup: Here’s what you need to know Squawk on the Street Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes. On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget. She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady." Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways." Peter Rice, seen here on May 3, 2017, was head of Disney's TV entertainment business in 2020. He was one of several executives passed over for the CEO job in favor of Chapek. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce. The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years. "We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday. Flagging engagement In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote. Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. "If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again." What Rice brings to Netflix Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms. Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade. With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring." Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October. Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast . "[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem." headlines.summary: SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced critical questions from the New York City Council on Friday.
headlines.article_text: SpaceX policy manger grilled by NYC Council on Grok AI safety, images Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced questions about Grok's generation of sexualized images from the New York City Council on Friday. NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin asked why she was able to pull up sexualized images of herself when Castillo Madrid said Grok does not let users create such images of real people. Elon Musk's aerospace and AI company previously evaded a subpoena to testify as part of a legislative investigation and hearing held last week. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The SpaceX headquarters is seen on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026 in Hawthorne, CA. Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images SpaceX artificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin and other members on Friday as part of a council investigation into AI safety. When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her. "I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?" Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance. NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent. "I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable." Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video. Elon Musk's aerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council to appear alongside leaders from OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and Meta on Oct. 5. SpaceX agreed to testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations. Read more CNBC tech news Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to her LinkedIn profile . Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce. De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any. "I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said. "I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something." Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety. Kim began his testimony before the council by outlining his experience as one of the first employees at xAI, saying that he "built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok." Kim said that he started raising concerns in January 2025 and those worries were shut down by his manager. "My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless, and that AI would kill us and all anyways," he said. Kim appeared by video, along with his attorney, following Castillo Madrid's questioning. Regarding Grok-generated images, Kim said under prior standards at the company, "tasteful nudity was acceptable and is the goal." "During my time there, there were only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned," Kim said. "And I think in large part due to the frustration with how safety was being handled." The council also pressed Castillo Madrid about other areas of misuse with Grok and the types of safeguards that were in place. Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied. SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not." Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies. "You're supposed to give us answers. You're not," she said. In merging SpaceX with xAI in February, Musk combined his AI and social networking business with his rocket launch company, which also owns the Starlink satellite internet service. The merger put SpaceX in control of AI model Grok, which is used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon . SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at about $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor. In skipping the earlier NYC Council hearing, SpaceX avoided direct questioning from a member of the U.K. Parliament, Jess Asato, who testified about experiencing AI-enabled online harassment. Asato is suing xAI in the U.K. after Grok users created and distributed sexualized images of her online without her consent. She's seeking damages, alleging misuse of her private information and breaches of European data protection rules. According to the BBC , Asato criticized SpaceX for its "arrogance" in not appearing last week. SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment ahead of the meeting. headlines.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
headlines.summary: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo is drawing early demand as analysts assess whether the foldable can lift iPhone pricing and revenue.
headlines.article_text: Apple iPhone Duo demand, pricing and revenue impact Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers, and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:19 02:19 First impressions of the iPhone Duo — Apple's biggest iPhone redesign ever News Videos Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the pre-order demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Apple CEO John Ternus, alongside vice president of industrial design Molly Anderson, shows off the new iPhone Duo during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, on September 9, 2026. Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty Images Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent TIME profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered an 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. Low volume, high value IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025. But the more important number for Apple may not be units. A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more. Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone. The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years. "Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC. The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added. It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup. Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price." Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.
